executive_summary: Today's intelligence picture is dominated by a converging threat against Western critical infrastructure, with state-aligned actors — particularly Russian and Iranian-linked groups — actively targeting energy and water systems across the U.S., Poland, and Ukraine through both conventional intrusion methods and novel attack vectors like private APNs, suggesting a coordinated effort to probe and degrade infrastructure resilience ahead of potential escalation. The cyber and ICS threats are compounded by a structural vulnerability problem: small U.S. utilities remain chronically under-resourced, and while the Senate funding proposal and the DEF CON-backed support center represent meaningful responses, they are reactive to a threat that is already inside the perimeter. Separately, a thread of strategic repositioning runs through the geopolitical and military reporting — the U.S. Indo-Pacific Command rename, DARPA's hypersonic missile program, armed drone testing in Korea, and the Virginia-class submarine optimized for seabed operations collectively signal an accelerating competition with China and potential adversaries in contested domains, even as the abrupt relief of the V Corps commander in Europe and unresolved questions around military budget integrity introduce friction into U.S. readiness at a sensitive moment. The inclusion of Chinese-made components in Royal Navy autonomous vessels and AI integration into nuclear command structures ties these threads together into a broader picture of supply chain exposure and escalation risk in an environment where arms control frameworks are eroding

sections.title: Cyber
sections.intro: Critical infrastructure faces coordinated pressure across multiple fronts, with a new ransomware-as-a-service operation drawing joint government warnings and a Russian military hacking campaign targeting Ukrainian IT professionals.

items.headline: FBI and South Korea issue joint warning on Gunra ransomware targeting critical infrastructure via firewall vulnerabilities
items.summary: CISA, the FBI, and South Korean authorities jointly warned that Gunra, a ransomware-as-a-service operation that emerged in 2025 and scaled up in 2026, is breaching critical infrastructure and government networks by exploiting vulnerabilities in widely-used firewall products. Affiliates employ double-extortion tactics, combining data theft with encryption. The joint advisory signals Gunra has reached a threat tier warranting multi-nation response, and organizations running affected firewall products should treat patching as urgent.
items.source: All CISA Advisories / The Record from Recorded Future News

items.headline: Sandworm hackers impersonate job recruiters to compromise Ukrainian IT sector
items.summary: Russia's GRU-linked Sandworm unit has been running a sustained social engineering campaign since at least May, posing as recruiters to lure Ukrainian IT workers and gain footholds in their systems, according to CERT-UA. Targeting technical staff—rather than traditional phishing of end users—suggests an intent to access developer environments or sensitive infrastructure. The campaign reflects an ongoing Russian effort to degrade Ukrainian cyber capacity through human-layer exploitation rather than purely technical intrusion.
items.source: The Record from Recorded Future News

items.headline: Poland reveals second hidden cyberattack on energy infrastructure linked to broader January offensive
items.summary: Polish authorities uncovered a previously undisclosed cyberattack on a heat plant that occurred simultaneously with a coordinated strike against more than 30 renewable energy installations, an incident only publicly acknowledged in January. The months-long concealment of the second intrusion raises questions about the full scope of the campaign and whether additional compromises remain undetected. The pattern points to a systematic targeting of Polish energy infrastructure, likely tied to broader hybrid pressure against NATO's eastern flank.
items.source: The Record from Recorded Future News

items.headline: US Senate Democrats propose $300 million annual fund to harden water sector cybersecurity
items.summary: Two Senate Democrats introduced legislation that would direct $300 million per year toward cybersecurity upgrades for water and wastewater utilities, a sector widely identified as critically under-resourced against cyber threats. The bill arrives as attacks on critical infrastructure are accelerating globally, and water systems—often running legacy operational technology—remain among the most exposed. Whether the legislation advances in a divided Congress will determine if it translates from signal into meaningful funding.
items.source: The Record from Recorded Future News

sections.title: Geopolitical
sections.intro: Global fault lines are sharpening across the Middle East, Europe's southern flank, and the Indian Ocean as diplomatic frameworks strain and regional actors test boundaries.

items.headline: Netanyahu Rejects Trump-Backed Gaza Deal, Extending Regional Deadlock
items.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu has blocked a Trump-mediated Gaza agreement, prolonging the conflict with no resolution in sight. The rejection signals a widening gap between Washington and Jerusalem on war termination terms, undermining U.S. leverage as a broker. Watch whether Trump applies meaningful pressure or absorbs the rebuff without consequence.

items.headline: Morocco Uses Ceuta Migration Crisis to Signal Strategic Leverage Over Spain
items.summary: A surge of migrants into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta has exposed Madrid's precarious geopolitical position, with Morocco using migration flows as a pressure instrument in its broader relationship with Spain and the EU. The episode illustrates how Rabat has become adept at weaponizing border management to extract political concessions. Madrid's limited response options reflect a wider European vulnerability to coercive migration tactics by North African partners.

items.headline: U.S. Indo-Pacific Command Rename Signals Reduced Indian Ocean Focus at a Critical Moment
items.summary: The reversion to 'U.S. Pacific Command' is largely symbolic in organizational terms but carries a significant signaling cost, suggesting diminished U.S. attention to the Indian Ocean precisely as China expands naval presence there and regional partners seek reassurance. Persistent uncertainty around basing and the closure of key installations compound the credibility gap. Allies in South Asia and East Africa will be watching whether the name change foreshadows real capability drawdowns.

items.headline: AI Integration into Nuclear Command Structures Raises Escalation Risk as Arms Control Erodes
items.summary: With New START expired, China on track to triple its warhead count by 2035, and Russia developing novel delivery systems, the nuclear landscape is deteriorating rapidly. The emerging overlay of AI-assisted decision-making into these dynamics introduces new failure modes, including faster escalation cycles and reduced human oversight at critical junctures. The absence of active arms control dialogue between major powers means these risks are accumulating without a diplomatic safety net.

sections.title: Military
sections.intro: Today's military picture spans procurement accountability failures, accelerating unmanned and hypersonic weapons development, and a significant leadership shake-up in Europe.

items.headline: GAO contradicts DOGE's $1.7B savings claim on military health IT contract
items.summary: DOGE publicly claimed $1.76 billion in savings from terminating a military health IT contract, but a GAO review found the contract was never actually terminated and no funds were deobligated. The discrepancy raises serious questions about the reliability of DOGE's reported savings figures across the federal government. Watch for congressional scrutiny and whether other claimed savings face similar audits.

items.headline: DARPA launches hypersonic cruise missile program to penetrate advanced air defenses
items.summary: DARPA is actively developing a hypersonic cruise missile designed to defeat increasingly capable enemy air defense systems, reflecting Pentagon concern that current U.S. strike missiles are becoming vulnerable to peer-competitor defenses. The program parallels Lockheed's Next Generation Interceptor passing two key design tests despite an 18-month delay due to motor issues, signaling simultaneous investment in both hypersonic offense and missile defense. The convergence of these programs underscores a broadening competition in long-range strike and defeat capabilities.

items.headline: U.S. forces test armed drones in Korea while Army pursues 50mm counter-drone cannon
items.summary: U.S. soldiers and Marines conducted live-ordnance drone weaponization drills in South Korea last week, reflecting the Army's push to embed unmanned attack capabilities across all formations. Simultaneously, the Army is soliciting industry proposals for a 50mm cannon system capable of defeating a wide range of drone threats. Together, these efforts signal a dual-track approach to drone warfare: fielding offensive UAS capacity while hardening ground forces against the same threat.

items.headline: Army abruptly relieves V Corps commander in Europe
items.summary: Lt. Gen. Charles Costanza was suddenly removed from command of V Corps, the U.S. Army's forward-deployed headquarters in Europe, with no immediate public explanation provided. The timing is notable given ongoing NATO commitments and the operational significance of the European theater. The lack of transparency around the dismissal will draw attention to the circumstances and potential command climate issues within one of the Army's most strategically positioned formations.

sections.title: Intel / OSINT
sections.intro: Today's intelligence picture is shaped by emerging ransomware threats to critical infrastructure, a specialized U.S. Navy seabed espionage capability, and ISR vulnerabilities at a key strategic outpost.

items.headline: FBI and South Korea issue joint warning on Gunra ransomware gang exploiting firewall vulnerabilities
items.summary: The Gunra ransomware group is actively targeting critical infrastructure by exploiting known vulnerabilities in widely deployed firewall products, prompting a rare joint advisory from the FBI and South Korean authorities. The gang's focus on critical infrastructure elevates the risk profile beyond typical ransomware incidents, suggesting potential for significant service disruption. Organizations running affected firewall brands should treat patch application as urgent and audit for indicators of compromise.
items.source: The Record from Recorded Future News

items.headline: U.S. Navy acquiring a modified Virginia-class submarine optimized for seabed intelligence and sabotage missions
items.summary: One Block V Virginia-class boat is being configured specifically for undersea intelligence collection and infrastructure sabotage operations on the seafloor, a highly specialized mission set that signals growing U.S. investment in subsea domain awareness and covert action. The capability directly mirrors concerns about adversary interference with undersea cables and pipelines. Watch for how this platform's development influences NATO and partner-nation seabed security doctrine.

items.headline: Unidentified drones spotted over Diego Garcia amid heightened U.S.-Iran tensions
items.summary: Multiple drone sightings have been reported over Diego Garcia, one of the U.S. military's most strategically sensitive remote bases, raising concerns about surveillance or pre-attack reconnaissance at a moment of sharply elevated hostility with Iran. The island hosts critical long-range strike and logistics assets, making it a high-value intelligence target. The incidents underscore the growing threat of maritime-launched drone operations against isolated, hard-to-defend installations.

items.headline: Chinese-made components in Royal Navy autonomous surface vessel raise supply chain intelligence concerns
items.summary: Chinese hardware embedded in the Royal Navy's new drone boat program has surfaced as a cybersecurity concern, highlighting the persistent difficulty of enforcing clean supply chains in defense procurement. The issue is analytically significant because such components could theoretically enable remote access, data exfiltration, or operational disruption by Beijing. This case is likely to accelerate UK and allied scrutiny of component-level provenance across unmanned military platforms.

sections.title: ICS / SCADA / OT
sections.intro: Water infrastructure dominates today's ICS threat landscape, with Iranian-linked attacks expanding across U.S. states while a novel network pivot technique was used to sabotage Polish energy facilities.

items.headline: Iranian-Linked Hackers Hit Water ICS in at Least 12 U.S. States, Including New Jersey and Alabama
items.summary: Threat actors with ties to Iran targeted industrial control systems at water utilities across a dozen U.S. states, with New Jersey and Alabama among the latest confirmed victims. The campaign underscores persistent adversary interest in attacking critical water infrastructure ICS, where internet-exposed PLCs and HMIs remain common. Watch for CISA guidance and whether any facilities experienced operational disruption beyond initial access.

items.headline: Hackers Used Private APN as Novel Attack Vector to Sabotage Second Polish Energy Facility
items.summary: CERT.PL has documented what it describes as the first known instance of a private Access Point Name (APN) — a cellular network channel used for remote ICS connectivity — being weaponized as an attack vector to compromise a second Polish energy facility. The technique allows attackers to pivot through legitimate-looking mobile network infrastructure, bypassing conventional perimeter defenses. This represents a meaningful expansion of the OT threat actor playbook and warrants immediate review of private APN usage in industrial environments.

items.headline: Small U.S. Water Utilities Chronically Under-Resourced as Cyber Threats Intensify
items.summary: An in-depth analysis highlights the structural cybersecurity deficit facing small water and wastewater utilities: aging ICS infrastructure, skeleton IT staffing, and minimal funding leave thousands of systems exposed to exactly the kind of attacks now being carried out against the sector. The gap is systemic rather than incidental, making broad remediation difficult without federal intervention. The concurrent launch of DEF CON Franklin's Water Watch Center and New York's $9 million SECURE grant program signal growing recognition of the problem, but coverage remains far from universal.

items.headline: DEF CON Franklin and Rural Water Association Launch Dedicated Cyber Support Center for Small Utilities
items.summary: The Water Watch Center, a joint initiative between DEF CON Franklin and the National Rural Water Association, aims to deliver direct cybersecurity assistance to small water utilities that lack internal security capabilities. The timing is significant given the active Iranian ICS targeting campaign and the documented resource gap across the sector. Success will depend on whether the center can scale outreach to the thousands of utilities currently operating with no meaningful cyber defense posture.
